Explain the three-act structure and its variations used in Hollywood screenwriting.

The three-act structure is the foundational architecture of Western narrative film. Act 1 (Setup, ~25% runtime): Establish ordinary world, introduce protagonist, inciting incident disrupts ordinary world, protagonist makes decision at plot point 1 that ends Act 1. Act 2 (Confrontation, ~50%): protagonist pursues goal against escalating obstacles, midpoint shifts direction or raises stakes significantly, dark night of the soul / all-is-lost moment near end of act, plot point 2 launches into Act 3. Act 3 (Resolution, ~25%): climax confrontation, resolution of all narrative threads, denouement. Variations: Save the Cat (Blake Snyder) breaks this into 15 beats with precise page counts — more formulaic but useful for commercial scripts. Five-act structure (TV drama — Breaking Bad, The Wire): each act ends on a hook, allows more breathing room for character development. Non-linear structures: in medias res opening (Memento, Pulp Fiction), frame narratives, multiple timelines. The Hero's Journey (Campbell/Vogler) maps mythological structure over three acts. Anti-structure: European art cinema often rejects clear act breaks (Antonioni, Tarkovsky) — character revelation replaces plot mechanics. Genre modifies the structure: horror inciting incident comes earlier, comedy has strict set-piece requirements at specific beats.

What makes Kubrick's visual language distinct and how did he achieve it?

Stanley Kubrick's visual grammar is defined by mathematical precision, psychological geometry, and a cold observational gaze. Key elements: Symmetrical composition: Kubrick used perfect bilateral symmetry extensively (the Overlook Hotel corridors, Alex's bedroom in Clockwork Orange, the war room in Dr. Strangelove) — creates unease and artificial order that suggests forces beyond human control. One-point perspective: camera placed on central axis with converging lines leading to vanishing point (the axe chase corridor, the hedge maze, military barracks in Full Metal Jacket) — simultaneously draws viewer in and creates claustrophobic compression. Kubrick zoom: slow forward dolly combined with slow zoom out (or vice versa) creates 'vertigo' effect where background and foreground move at different rates — used in Barry Lyndon and The Shining. Barry Lyndon's natural light cinematography: Kubrick used NASA-developed f/0.7 lenses modified by Zeiss to shoot entirely by candlelight — 18th century paintings brought to life. Long Steadicam tracking shots (Shining — OB-WAN scenes): immersive but slightly wrong, creating dread through fluid pursuit. Kubrick's obsessive research translated into productions that took years — Full Metal Jacket shot over 400 days. His visual choices always served psychological theme: the perfect compositions represent the dehumanizing forces (war, capitalism, madness) his films examine.

Explain cinematography lens choices — focal length, depth of field, and psychological effect.

Focal length fundamentally changes how a viewer perceives space and subjects: Wide angle (14-35mm): Exaggerates perspective depth, foreground appears larger relative to background, slight distortion at extremes. Psychological effect: expands space, creates environment emphasis, at extreme wide angles (8-14mm) creates distortion that suggests psychological distortion or forced perspective (Citizen Kane's deep focus, Dr. Caligari expressionist influence). Used for chase sequences, action, establishing expansive environments. Normal (40-60mm): Closest to human eye perception, no distortion, natural space. Creates documentary realism (Dardenne brothers, Dogme 95). Psychological neutrality. Telephoto (85-400mm+): Compresses space, makes foreground and background appear at similar distance, shallow depth of field. 85-105mm: flattering for portraiture, slight compression. 135mm: Gordon Willis's 'Prince of Darkness' lens — Godfather shots that isolate subjects. 300-400mm: surveillance feeling, celebrity paparazzi quality. Used by Vilmos Zsigmond for McCabe & Mrs. Miller — telephoto through snowstorms creates impressionistic distance. Depth of field: shallow DoF (wide aperture) isolates subject from background, directs attention, intimate or voyeuristic. Deep DoF (stop down) — Citizen Kane's revolutionary deep focus (Gregg Toland, f/3.5 throughout with composite mattes) — all planes in focus simultaneously, camera doesn't need to reveal what's important.

What is the cinematographic philosophy of Roger Deakins and how does light define his work?

Roger Deakins ASC BSC is widely considered the greatest living cinematographer. His philosophy centers on motivated lighting — every light source in frame should appear to come from a real-world source (window, lamp, fire, screen), even when artificial. Key techniques: Practicals integration: Deakins obsesses over practical light sources in frame. The prisoners' flames in Shawshank, the office fluorescents in Blade Runner 2049, the burning windmill in True Grit. The practical light motivates the artificial light that actually illuminates the scene. No Lights approach: on 1917, Deakins and director Sam Mendes designed the production so that natural light was maximized — they built the trenches and environments to allow natural light to work. Collaboration with production design: Deakins always works closely with PD to ensure practical sources are positioned correctly for camera. Blade Runner 2049 visual language: Deakins and Denis Villeneuve agreed on a color-coded world — each location has a distinct color palette (orange dust, white snow, grey city). Lighting never decorative — always expresses the psychological state of characters. 1917 one-shot technique: demanded extremely precise lighting design since camera couldn't stop. Mixed practicals (natural light, fire torches) with pre-rigged LED panels hidden in environment. His career spans Coen Brothers (every film since Barton Fink), No Country for Old Men's stark naturalism, Shawshank's warmth, Sicario's bleached-out border violence.

Explain the visual storytelling language of color in cinema.

Color in film functions as an emotional subtext layer operating below conscious narrative. Primary approaches: Symbolic color coding: specific colors carry consistent meaning within a film's world (not universal — culturally and contextually determined). Red in Schindler's List: the girl's red coat is the only color in the black-and-white film — isolates innocence against systematic extermination. Blue in Moonlight: coolness, beauty, outside world, sexual awakening — cinematographer James Laxton's blue-green palette vs warm skin tones. Color arc / transformation: protagonist's color association changes as character changes. In Amélie (Bruno Delbonnel): warm amber-yellow world of Paris reflects Amélie's enchanted perspective — when she withdraws, cooler tones. In Three Colors trilogy (Kieslowski + Slawomir Idziak/Piotr Sobocinski): Blue/White/Red directly embody the concepts they explore. Desaturation for realism or psychological withdrawal: Saving Private Ryan's desaturated, bleached-out palette (Janusz Kaminski) — war drains color from life. Traffic's three color-coded storylines each have distinct palette — green for Mexico, yellow-grey for US drug plot, blue for suburban story. Complementary color contrast: orange/teal (ubiquitous in Hollywood blockbusters via DI grading — warm skin tones against teal shadows). Production design + costume + lighting must coordinate for cohesive color language. Director of Photography and production designer must establish color bible in pre-production.

What separates great screenwriting dialogue from average dialogue?

Great cinematic dialogue serves character revelation, subtext, and plot simultaneously while sounding natural — a paradox since people in real life rarely speak with such precision. Character revelation through diction: every character should have a distinct voice determined by their education, background, psychological state, desire. Mamet's characters speak in clipped, rhythmic patterns that reveal status games and power dynamics. The Coen Brothers' characters use hyper-specific regional speech (Fargo's Minnesotan cadences, No Country's sparse Texas reticence). Subtext — saying one thing meaning another: professional screenplay dialogue rarely states emotional content directly. Characters talk around what they want. In Before Sunrise, Celine and Jesse discuss other things while conducting the most important conversation of their lives. In Inherent Vice, the comedy comes from characters who speak elliptically around paranoid realities. 'No dialogue should mean exactly what it says' — the deeper meaning creates dramatic irony when audience understands what characters are avoiding. Conflict embedded: every scene of dialogue should have competing wants — each character wants something different from the conversation. The dialogue is the battlefield. Economical exposition: bad dialogue = 'As you know, Bob, we are scientists working on a top-secret project.' Good exposition is embedded in conflict, character behavior, or visual storytelling — the dialogue doesn't explain what the film can show. Specificity over generality: 'a 1967 Chevrolet Impala' over 'a car.' Specific details create world.

How does film editing shape emotion and meaning — explain the core principles.

Editing is the final rewrite — the editor determines what a film is. Core principles: Kuleshov Effect: the meaning of a shot changes based on what precedes and follows it. Pudovkin's experiments showed the same actor's face read as hunger, grief, or joy depending on adjacent shots. This is cinema's unique grammar. Cut on action: matching action across a cut creates continuity — the audience's eye follows movement across the edit, perceiving continuous space. Jump cut: Godard in Breathless made jump cuts famous — cuts within the same shot that violate continuity. Creates disorientation, energy, self-consciousness. L-cuts and J-cuts: audio leads or lags video — dialogue from next scene plays over image of current scene (L-cut), or vice versa (J-cut). Creates fluid transitions, bridges emotional states. Intercutting / cross-cutting: parallel editing between simultaneous events creates tension (Griffith's last-minute rescue), thematic juxtaposition (the christening / murders in Godfather), irony (Eisenstein's October). Rhythm: cut timing creates tempo — fast cuts in action create excitement, held shots create unease or contemplation. Tarkovsky holds shots beyond comfort. The Revenant's editing rhythm mimics trauma — disorienting, unpredictable. Invisible editing ideal: classical Hollywood wanted editing to be unnoticed. Continuity editing rules (180-degree rule, match on action) exist to maintain this illusion. Breaking rules draws attention to the medium itself — Godard, Bergman, Bresson used visible editing as statement.

What is the Dogme 95 movement and what did it contribute to cinema?

Dogme 95 was a radical filmmaking manifesto created by Lars von Trier and Thomas Vinterberg in Copenhagen in 1995. The 'Vow of Chastity' had 10 rules: shooting on location (no artificial sets), diegetic sound only (no score added in post), handheld camera, color film (no special lighting), no genre conventions (murder, weapons), no superficial action (no stunts), no temporal/spatial alienation, no director credit on film. Philosophy: strip cinema of artifice and illusion to expose raw truth. Counter-reaction against Hollywood spectacle and auteur cinema's fetishism of visual style. Key films: Festen (Vinterberg, 1998) — filmed on early consumer DV camera at a family celebration where abuse is revealed. The Celebration's raw DV texture made the psychological exposure feel documentary. Idioterne (von Trier, 1998) — deliberately provocative. Impact on cinema: democratized filmmaking — DV cameras meant anyone could make a Dogme film. Influenced the entire movement toward digital naturalism. Direct precursor to: Mumblecore movement (Swanberg, Duplass brothers), contemporary naturalistic acting styles, the 'dogmatic' approaches of Dardenne brothers (though predating Dogme). The rules were eventually violated by the founders themselves — Dogme was more polemical provocation than lasting constraint. Its real contribution: proved that technical limitation breeds creative freedom and that emotional truth could overwhelm technical polish.
